sentences.text: Of the fine awarded, Rs.45,000/- has been directed to be paid to the victim through her mother.
Against that sentence awarded, the appellant remained confined for about 22 years.
3. The Sessions Trial emerged on the F.I.R. dated 30.09.2001, lodged by 'H', the mother of the victim 'X'.
She is PW-1 at the trial.
The F.I.R. was registered as Case Crime No.249 of 2001.
It is Ex.Ka-7 at the trial.
It arose from the Written Report submitted by 'H' dated 30.09.2001.
It is Ex.Ka-1 at the trial.
The scribe of the F.I.R. was one Pawan Kumar (not examined at the trial).
The F.I.R. narrates, 'H' was living with her husband (the appellant), the victim 'X' aged about 14 years and her son 'J' (not examined at the trial).
On 20.08.2001, the appellant administered some intoxicating substance to 'H' and 'X' during night and thereafter committed rape on 'X'.
He also threatened 'X' not to tell anyone about that occurrence.
Thereafter, the appellant committed repeated rape on 'X'.
Last on 28.09.2001, at about 2:30 a.m., the appellant committed rape on 'X'.
'H' caught him at that time.
The appellant prayed for mercy.
On her query, the victim disclosed to 'H' that the appellant had earlier committed rape on her on many occasions.
Such facts were disclosed by 'H' to her neighbours.
On such development, the appellant became belligerent and claimed that he was the father of 'X' and he may do with her, as he pleases.
That filled others with fear.
They backed out.
Thereafter, the appellant continued to threaten 'H'.

For that reason, the F.I.R.
narrated, she lodged the F.I.R. with some delay.
4. Upon such F.I.R. being registered, statement of 'X' was recorded on 04.10.2001.
It is Ex.Ka-2 at the trial.
In that statement she disclosed her age to be 14 years.
She claimed, she had been subjected to rape by the appellant from 20.08.2001 onwards.
In that she disclosed that the appellant used to sprinkle some medicine over 'X' and 'H' causing them to fall asleep.
Thereafter, he would treat her as his wife.
She further claimed, at the relevant time, she was not aware of the occurrence/s.
On waking in the next morning, she discovered the draw string of her lower wear/ 'salwar' undone.
She further proved that the appellant used to follow her inside the house.
He also molested her by placing his hands on her chest and her private parts.
He also beat her and threatened her to not tell her mother or other siblings about the occurrence.
In that, he threatened 'X', he would set the house on fire, if she told anyone about the occurrence.
During night hours, he would command 'X' to keep quiet and take her to another room of the house.
She further narrated, after about four days from the occurrence on 20.08.2001, 'H' had enquired from the appellant what he was upto (with 'X').
To that he replied-nothing.
When 'H' came to know about the occurrence and confronted the appellant with the same, he threatened to set the house on fire, unless, he was allowed to have its way with 'X'.
All efforts made by 'H' to make the appellant understand the situation, failed.
In fact, once the appellant sprinkled kerosene oil in the room and set a piece of paper to fire, set the house ablaze.

That was put off by 'H'.
5.
At that stage, 'X' further stated that the tenants of the parties also tried to intervene with the appellant, on her behalf, but to no avail.
In such circumstances, she disclosed, the appellant committed repeated rape on her.
On 28.09.2001 at about 2:00-2:30 a.m., after the appellant had administered intoxicating substance to 'X' and committed rape on her.

Upon a power outage, 'H'
tugged her braid, but 'X' could not respond.
Then, 'H' made the appellant get off 'X'.
The appellant did not heed to counselling of 'H'.
He quarrelled.

Therefore, 'H' lodged the F.I.R.

10. Thereafter, the statement of appellant was recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
The defence led no evidence.
11. Thereafter, the Court below heard the parties and passed the order of conviction and punishment as noted above.
12. Learned Amicus Curiae submits, the prosecution story is inherently false and improbable.
The appellant served the Indian Army.
He retired from service barely an year before the occurrence.
While the prosecution describes that the occurrence was caused between 20.08.2001 to 28/29.09.2001, the F.I.R. was lodged on 30.09.2001.
In that, it was disclosed, 'H' first came to know of the occurrence on 28/29.09.2001 itself whereas 'X' had been suffering such occurrences from 20.08.2001.
Thus, improbability has been suggested in the occurrence as narrated based on the account offered by 'H' and 'X' being mother and daughter.

13. To support his submission, it has further been submitted that it has come on record by way of prosecution evidence that there was no prior occurrence of such nature was ever caused by the appellant or suffered by 'X'.

It has also come on record by way of prosecution evidence that prior to the occurrence, the appellant had constructed the house for his family wherein he along with 'H', 'X'
and 'J' were living.
During his days in service, for reason of being posted at far off places, he used to send Rs.3,000/- per month to 'H'.
In absence of any other conduct alleged or proven, the present prosecution story emerged only because of other differences that arose, after the appellant retired from service.

14. No proof was offered of any medicine or intoxicating substance ever administered to 'X' or to 'H'
as may have rendered them unconscious.
No recovery whatsoever was made of any such substance.

In absence of that fact proven, a highly improbable and unbelievable account has been offered by the prosecution, wherein it has been disclosed, the appellant had been committing rape on his daughter, in the small house, where all his family resided.
15. Third, it has been submitted that bad relations between 'H' and her in-laws i.e. close blood relatives of the appellant was proven on the strength of prosecution.
Therefore, 'H' had every motive to make a false accusation against the appellant to deprive him of the house property and gain exclusive rights therein.

16. Next, it has been submitted that the appellant was not present at the time and place of occurrence on 28/29.09.2001, inasmuch as after his retirement from Indian Army, had been re-employed as a Security Guard.

sentences.text: Also, it has been submitted, the scribe of the FIR, Pawan Kumar was a local Corporator.
The FIR came to be lodged under his undue influence.
The investigation was also partisan.
The prosecution deliberately did not examine him to hide the prior motivation behind the false FIR.
18. Next, in the alternative, it has been submitted, life sentence awarded to the appellant is too heavy.

Commensurate aggravated circumstances had not been made out or proven by the prosecution as may warrant award of life sentence, but minimum sentence being prescribed by law being seven years (at the relevant time).

The appellant remained confined for almost 22 years before he was enlarged on bail earlier by this Court vide order dated 05.10.2023.
19.
On the other hand, learned A.G.A. submitted, the prosecution story was clearly narrated in the FIR.
That FIR was lodged promptly within two days from the day 'H', who is the mother of the victim of 'X', gained knowledge of the occurrence.
If at all required, both 'H' and 'X' proved and thus explained the circumstances in which the FIR may not have been lodged earlier.

Thus, it was explained, that on 'H' confronting the appellant of his wrong doing and requiring him to refrain from causing such occurrences, he became belligerent and threatened 'X' and 'H' as also others (relatives neighbours and tenants) with dire consequences.
He also threatened to set the house ablaze.
In such proven facts, it would have taken time, effort and courage both on part of 'H' and also on the victim 'X', to lodge the FIR.

20. As to the plea of inherent falsity/improbability set up on behalf of the appellant, it has been averred, in sexual offences, unless the prosecution story is found to be inherently improbable, such inference may not be readily drawn.
Here, the prosecution story was proven on the strength of cogent evidence led by 'H' and the victim 'X'.

Despite lengthy cross-examination of all those witnesses, by the appellant (himself), no doubt emerged either as to the fact that the occurrence was first caused on 20.08.2001 or that it was repeated till 28/29.09.2001.
Those facts being proven, the prosecution case may be tested on such evidence and not on vague general probabilities being voiced.
Such probabilities may be based on notions of morality but not on facts proven at the trial.
21. Third, it has been stated, merely because the scribe of the FIR may not have been examined at the trial, it may not cause any credible defect on the prosecution story.
In any case, according to the appellant, the scribe, namely, Pavan Kumar was a Corporator.
Being a public representative he may have been approached by 'H' in the circumstances in which she may have found herself.
For reason of FIR written by the said Pavan Kumar, no doubt may be raised in the prosecution story.
To the extent, 'H' duly proved the submission of the Written Report and the registration of the FIR was also proven on such Written Report, non-examination of the scribe is of no consequence.
22. Next, it has been argued, the plea of alibi was never proven.
The burden lay squarely on the appellant to prove that plea.
Therefore, the learned court below has rightly disbelieved the same.
23. Further, it has been submitted, existence of bad relations between 'H' and her in-laws is also of no consequence.
She neither made any allegation against her in-laws nor she stood to gain on her in-laws by making false accusation against the present appellant.

sentences.text: Last, it has been argued, the appellant being father of the victim of 'X', who was a minor below 16 years of age on the time of occurrence, no leniency may be observed in the award of sentence inasmuch as the father is a person, who enjoys absolute trust of his children.
Having committed "aggravated penetrative sexual assault" on his minor daughter, the appellant has been rightly sentenced for life.

25. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and having perused the record, in the first place,
there is no material departure from the story as narrated by the first informant 'H' in the FIR and as proven by the prosecution, at the trial.

In the Written Report giving rise to the FIR itself, 'H' had disclosed that her minor daughter 'X' aged about 14 years had been subjected to repeated rape by her father, the present appellant from 20.08.2001 to 28.09.2001 i.e. for more than a month.

As to such occurrences, it was disclosed, the appellant used to administer (by sprinkling), some intoxicating substance to 'H' and to 'X' after they went to sleep and thereafter he used to commit the offence, when 'X' had no control over herself.
As to the discovery of such occurrence, 'H' further disclosed, she first saw the appellant commit such occurrence upon 'X' on 28/29.09.2001 at about 2.30 a.m.
At that time, she pulled him away from over 'X'.
The appellant offered an apology to 'H'.
However, on further inquiries 'X' revealed to 'H' that such occurrence had been caused by the appellant on earlier occasions as well.

When 'H' along with her neighbours confronted the appellant,
the next morning, he became belligerent and threatened to do as he would please, with his daughter ('X').
On that, the neighbours retreated.
Similar facts were proven by 'H' at the trial, during her examination-in-chief.
She further elaborated that on being first confronted, the appellant disowned his paternity over 'X' and claimed he would do as he pleased.
On his behaviour being further objected, he threatened to set the house on fire.
She also proved that the appellant usually caused such occurrences (on 'X'), during night as also day time, if he could find 'X' alone.
She also proved the fact that efforts were made on her part with the help of her neighbours and family to convince the appellant to refrain from such conduct.
Those efforts also met with failure.

In such circumstances, she proved that she lodged the FIR on 30.09.2001.
26.
During her extensive cross-examination, conducted over three days, no doubt emerged as to the facts proven by 'H'.

She was mostly questioned on the aspects not related to the occurrence, namely,
the quality of her relations with her in-laws and, the appellant and if she had earlier lived with the appellant during his years in service while he was posted outside.
Responses to those questioning may largely remain irrelevant to the occurrence.
As to the relations enjoyed by the appellant with his children and 'H', she stated, prior to that occurrence the appellant had not offered any objectionable conduct.
She learnt about the same on 28.09.2001 itself, as noted above.
She also disclosed normal husband-wife relationship enjoyed by her with the appellant.
At the same time, on being further questioned, she explained, all her family members slept in one room.
As to intoxicating substance administered, she disclosed, though it may not have been consumed by her and by 'X', the appellant may have sprayed the same, after 'X' and 'H' had gone off to sleep.

She also explained that for reason of such intoxicating substance thus administered on 'X' and 'H', they found it difficult to wake up,
the next morning.
27.
She was specifically questioned as to how she learnt of the occurrence on 28.09.2001.
She described - she heard a shriek of 'X'.

On that she saw 'X' was in a state of intoxication and was Satnam Singh vs State Of U.P. on 8 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199795124/
6 unable to resist the assault being made on her by the appellant.

sentences.text: 'H' pushed the appellant away from 'X'.
On that, the appellant got angry and started scolding her.
As to her previous statement, that she may have made before the police that on being thus reprimanded, the appellant had admitted his mistake, she denied having made such statement before the police.
28. Similarly, 'X' (P.W.-2) proved the occurrence of 28.09.2001 when at about 2.30 a.m., the appellant is described to have committed rape on her.
She disclosed, while that occurrence was being caused by the appellant, 'H' caught and pushed the appellant away from 'X'.
She also proved that 'H' reprimanded the appellant for such conduct on which the appellant started quarrelling with her.
In that, he insisted that he being the father of 'X' would do as he pleases, with 'X'.

Thereafter,
she proved that the occurrence was caused on 20.08.2001 and continued thereafter, on many occasions.

She further claimed that the appellant used to sprinkle some intoxicating substance before causing the occurrences and threatened 'X' that if she would inform 'H' about the occurrence,
he would kill her and others as well.

29. Further, she proved that on 29.09.2001 her maternal aunt as also her maternal grand-parents and neighbours had tried to persuade the appellant to refrain from committing such heinous offence on 'X'.
That effort met with refusal by the appellant.
At that stage, he insisted that 'X' was his daughter and he may do as he pleases with her.
He also threatened to kill anyone, who came in his way.
In view of such conduct offered, the relatives and neighbours retreated.
She also proved her earlier statement recorded under Section 164 Cr.P.C., wherein she had given similar description of the occurrence as was proven by her during her examination-in-chief.
30. On a cumulative assessment of the evidence of 'H' (P.W.-1) and 'X' (P.W.-2), we find no material difference in the two narrations offered by these prosecution witnesses.
Both are eye witnesses of the occurrence that took place on 28/29.09.2001.
One is the victim and the other was her mother and saviour.
She got up while the occurrence was being caused by the appellant on 28.09.2001 and had pushed the appellant away from 'X'.

Minor differences apart - as to whether the appellant had offered apology to 'H' on being first reprimanded on 28.09.2001, or not, and whether 'X' had let out a shriek that may have woken up 'H' or whether 'H' may have otherwise woken up, there is nothing to doubt the occurrence as proven by the two eye witnesses.

Here, we may also note that 'H' in her testimony has also proven the fact that for a few days she was suspecting something wrong with the appellant in his interaction with his daughter 'X' (when the two were seen seated together).
On questioning the appellant, he had not given a satisfactory reply and indicated that there was nothing going wrong.
Being a mother, it is wholly normal that she may have remained vigilant towards her daughter suspecting the appellant (the father of 'X') to be behaving improperly with 'X'.

Therefore, it is equally probable that she may have remained extra vigilant and may have been thus woken up at the slightest noise indicating something amiss with 'X', on 28.09.2001.
31.
On such proven facts, the delay in lodging the FIR stood wholly explained.

'X' was a minor, who may not be burdened to act with prudence and courage attributable to an adult - to promptly lodge an FIR against her father or to be in a position to state such information of the occurrence with her mother promptly.
Obviously, the minor had been violated by a person of trust.
It would have confused and befuddled at the occurrence suffered by her.

On top of that, she had been threatened Satnam Singh vs State Of U.P. on 8 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199795124/
7 with very dire consequences of death to all her family and her house being burnt, if she revealed the occurrence to anyone.

sentences.text: From the last occurrence i.e. 28.09.2001, (when the appellant was caught causing the occurrence by 'H', the mother of 'X'), the F.I.R. was lodged promptly.
The prosecution story progressed wholly naturally and with promptitude, thereafter.
The next day, the appellant was confronted by the near relatives of 'H' as also his neighbours.
Rather than, mending his ways (if he could), he turned belligerent and offered further threats.
It was proven though it was not required by the prosecution to prove, that on such belligerent conduct of the appellant, the relatives of 'H' and neighbours retreated.
Thus, the next day, the FIR came to be lodged.

Time taken to lodge the F.I.R.
is thus wholly natural and minimal.
It is wholly explained.
32. As to the non-examination of the scribe of the F.I.R., namely, Pavan Kumar, it is wholly immaterial as the Written Report was submitted by the informant 'H'.
It was duly proven at the trial.

The fact that Criminal Case was registered thereupon was also proven by P.W.-6, namely,
Rameshwar Tyagi.
Therefore, the doubt being raised on that count is wholly extraneous.
33. As to the plea of alibi, undoubtedly the burden lay on the defence to prove that fact.
Absolutely no evidence was led in that regard.
Therefore, that weak defence though raised, stands without any element of proof.
It does not merit any further consideration either by the learned court below or by this Court.
Bad relations allegedly suffered by 'H' with her in-laws is also a fact extraneous to the present proceeding.
Description of relations between a lady and her in-laws, as bad, is neither actionable nor descriptive of any real status of those relations.
To describe such relations as bad is a very subjective.
It conveys nothing.
Neither it suggests the degree of bad relations suffered nor it suggests any circumstance in which a person suffering from bad relations may be motivated to make a false accusation.

Neither any description whatsoever was given or proven by the defence that 'H'
stood to gain against her in-laws, by making a false accusation against the appellant nor it may lead to any fruitful result.

Though, 'H' proved, earlier her brother-in-law, who was a bachelor had laid a bad-eye on her, that occurrence was very old i.e. soon after her marriage when she used to live alone at the parental home of the appellant, while the appellant was posted outside at far away places,
while he was serving the Indian Army.

On the contrary, she specifically proved, since his retirement,
the appellant was living with his family in a four room house.
Also prior to the occurrence, she had not observed any objectionable behaviour offered by the appellant towards 'X' or any of his family members.
34. However, coming to the occurrence, all material facts were duly proven in the manner narrated by the prosecution.
First on 20.08.2001 and last on 28.09.2001, the appellant committed rape on 'X', his minor daughter.
What would motivate any human being to commit such a heinous offence, is not for the Court to explore, in the proven facts of this case.
Rape remains a crime of passion.
It inheres in it's description commission of the offence, in negation of prudent behaviour that is otherwise attributable to any human being.
What degree of imprudence the offender suffers, may motivate him to commit such offence against a minor or his own child, is not required to be examined in the proven facts of this case.

35. In view of such proven facts and upon consideration of submissions advanced by learned counsel for the parties, we do not find any good ground to interfere in the conviction order passed by the Satnam Singh vs State Of U.P. on 8 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199795124/

sentences.text: learned court below, merely because certain aspects of the prosecution story as narrated in the FIR and proven on the strength of ocular evidence, at the trial including as to sprinkling of intoxicating material may not have found corroborative evidence inasmuch as no intoxicating liquid or container/vessel was recovered during investigation
. It may not lead to any reasonable doubt in the prosecution story.
Unfortunate as it is, it remains a reality in our jurisprudence.
Such inaccuracies exist.
The Courts may remain bound to test the prosecution story guided by the 'ring of truth' test giving higher credence to the proven statement of injured witnesses, such as rape survivors.
In absence of any reasonable doubt raised to the prosecution story, we are not inclined to examine the issue any further.
Also, a presumption may always exist that such allegations may never be made against close family members especially fathers, unless the facts do give rise to such allegations.
No other fact of illicit relations of 'H' or 'X' was proven.
Plainly, there is no reason to doubt the prosecution story as proven at the trial.
As such, the order of conviction made by the learned court below is confirmed.
36. As to the sentence, it is clear that at the relevant time the only provision with respect to offence of rape existed was in the shape of Section 375 I.P.C. read with Section 376 I.P.C.
The minimum punishment that may have been awarded under that provision was seven years with maximum being life sentence, along with fine.
Considering the fact that the appellant has remained confined for 22 years (actual).
Award of life sentence is practically a sentence of imprisonment-till-dead.

Though, the facts are aggravating to the extent that the appellant is the father of 'X', who was minor,
we find that the appellant has undergone sufficient sentence as may not warrant any further imprisonment.
Accordingly, the sentence awarded to the appellant is modified from life imprisonment to the sentence already undergone by the appellant.
37. The appellant shall pay the balance fine of Rs.50,000/- for the offence within two months.
The same be paid out to 'X'.
In case fine is not deposited within the aforesaid period, appellant shall further undergo imprisonment of six months.
The appellant is on bail.
Upon payment of due fine, as above, sureties and bail bonds furnished by the appellant to be released on bail, shall stand discharged.
38. Accordingly, the appeal is partly allowed.

39. Let the trial court record along with a copy of this order be transmitted to the court concerned through Registrar (Compliance) forthwith and a copy of this order may also be sent to the C.J.M.,
concerned.
40.
C.J.M., concerned shall submit his compliance report in this regard to this Court.
41. A copy of this order be also sent to the Jail Authorities, concerned for necessary compliance.
42. Office is directed to take necessary steps to ensure that the name of the appellant is not commonly reflected in the computerised records of the Court - as is visible to the public.
Only in the event of certified copy of this order being applied for by the appellant (and not by others), the same may be issued disclosing the full name particulars of the appellant.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Here, the prosecution story was proven on the strength of cogent evidence led by 'H' and the victim 'X'.
Those facts being proven, the prosecution case may be tested on such evidence and not on vague general probabilities being voiced.
Such probabilities may be based on notions of morality but not on facts proven at the trial.
'X' was a minor, who may not be burdened to act with prudence and courage attributable to an adult - to promptly lodge an FIR against her father or to be in a position to state such information of the occurrence with her mother promptly.
Obviously, the minor had been violated by a person of trust.
It was proven though it was not required by the prosecution to prove, that on such belligerent conduct of the appellant, the relatives of 'H' and neighbours retreated.
Time taken to lodge the F.I.R.
is thus wholly natural and minimal.
It was duly proven at the trial.
33. As to the plea of alibi, undoubtedly the burden lay on the defence to prove that fact.
Absolutely no evidence was led in that regard.
Therefore, that weak defence though raised, stands without any element of proof.
Bad relations allegedly suffered by 'H' with her in-laws is also a fact extraneous to the present proceeding.
Description of relations between a lady and her in-laws, as bad, is neither actionable nor descriptive of any real status of those relations.
To describe such relations as bad is a very subjective.
It conveys nothing.
Neither it suggests the degree of bad relations suffered nor it suggests any circumstance in which a person suffering from bad relations may be motivated to make a false accusation.
Neither any description whatsoever was given or proven by the defence that 'H'
stood to gain against her in-laws, by making a false accusation against the appellant nor it may lead to any fruitful result.
Though, 'H' proved, earlier her brother-in-law, who was a bachelor had laid a bad-eye on her, that occurrence was very old i.e. soon after her marriage when she used to live alone at the parental home of the appellant, while the appellant was posted outside at far away places,
while he was serving the Indian Army.
On the contrary, she specifically proved, since his retirement,
the appellant was living with his family in a four room house.
Also prior to the occurrence, she had not observed any objectionable behaviour offered by the appellant towards 'X' or any of his family members.
First on 20.08.2001 and last on 28.09.2001, the appellant committed rape on 'X', his minor daughter.
What would motivate any human being to commit such a heinous offence, is not for the Court to explore, in the proven facts of this case.
Rape remains a crime of passion.
It inheres in it's description commission of the offence, in negation of prudent behaviour that is otherwise attributable to any human being.
What degree of imprudence the offender suffers, may motivate him to commit such offence against a minor or his own child, is not required to be examined in the proven facts of this case.
learned court below, merely because certain aspects of the prosecution story as narrated in the FIR and proven on the strength of ocular evidence, at the trial including as to sprinkling of intoxicating material may not have found corroborative evidence inasmuch as no intoxicating liquid or container/vessel was recovered during investigation
. It may not lead to any reasonable doubt in the prosecution story.
Unfortunate as it is, it remains a reality in our jurisprudence.
Such inaccuracies exist.
The Courts may remain bound to test the prosecution story guided by the 'ring of truth' test giving higher credence to the proven statement of injured witnesses, such as rape survivors.
Also, a presumption may always exist that such allegations may never be made against close family members especially fathers, unless the facts do give rise to such allegations.
No other fact of illicit relations of 'H' or 'X' was proven.
36. As to the sentence, it is clear that at the relevant time the only provision with respect to offence of rape existed was in the shape of Section 375 I.P.C. read with Section 376 I.P.C.
The minimum punishment that may have been awarded under that provision was seven years with maximum being life sentence, along with fine.
Considering the fact that the appellant has remained confined for 22 years (actual).
opennyai_summary.decision:
Award of life sentence is practically a sentence of imprisonment-till-dead.
Accordingly, the sentence awarded to the appellant is modified from life imprisonment to the sentence already undergone by the appellant.
37. The appellant shall pay the balance fine of Rs.50,000/- for the offence within two months.
The same be paid out to 'X'.
In case fine is not deposited within the aforesaid period, appellant shall further undergo imprisonment of six months.
The appellant is on bail.
Upon payment of due fine, as above, sureties and bail bonds furnished by the appellant to be released on bail, shall stand discharged.
38. Accordingly, the appeal is partly allowed.
39. Let the trial court record along with a copy of this order be transmitted to the court concerned through Registrar (Compliance) forthwith and a copy of this order may also be sent to the C.J.M.,
concerned.
